ZOOL . Raccoon, Procyon lotor. One of the oratas (kings) who met with Pardo’s 1566-1568 expedition in the town of Joara (Xuala) in the Appalachian Highlands was named Atuki, who was likely a Biloxi king named after this clever animal. This provides more linguistic evidence of ancestral Biloxi origins in the southern Appalachian region before migration to the Gulf Coast. It also likely indicates a Biloxi encounter with Europeans about years sooner than previously thought. (The usual date cited has been upon the Biloxis’ first meeting with the French on the Gulf Coast.) - ed

BOT . Grass, weed. cf., OP wathą́zi, Os wathą́zi, Tu mą • ta • xé • and mątasé. Possibly after copying the Caddoan word, Biloxi tąsi came to mean simply ‘grass’ (corn is a type of grass). The origin of the root form tąse or tąze is unknown, although it is worth noting that the Western Muskogean and MTL term for ‘corn’ is tąči. An archetype of this form seems to have been particularly widespread, even into the Puebloan SW: Kiowa a • thán ‘corn tassel’ and é • thâl ‘corn’ and Proto-Keresan *dâ • ni ‘squash.’ Muskogean oral histories state that they originally migrated from the west or Mexico (although this claim may be subject to geographical debate, since Mexico once covered a much larger portion of the western US). However, perhaps the spread of this tąsi-like term from the SW to the northern Gulf and Eastern Seaboard suggests that the term, and perhaps the cultigen, came via a migration and may give us clues to this migratory route from the SW to the east by Muskogeans or others. -ed
